# `golden/ingest/` — the ingest fixture set (TASK-151)

Fixtures for the upload/paste ingest pipeline: the magic-byte sniff, the
header dimension read, the pre-decode pixel guard, the HEIC transcode and the
EXIF/XMP/GPS strip.

They are **committed** and read from disk by the tests. The synthetic ones are
generated by [`generate.mjs`](./generate.mjs), which is run **by hand** and
never at test time. A fixture generated at test time can drift with its
generator and still agree with it — the same vacuous agreement `T-SEC-032e`
exists to prevent.

Load them through [`index.ts`](./index.ts) and assert on them through
[`exifProbe.ts`](./exifProbe.ts). Never `readFileSync` one directly: the loader
is what turns a lost owner-supplied fixture into a loud, named failure instead
of a silent one.

## Licence and provenance

Every synthetic file here was generated by `generate.mjs` in this repository.
**Nothing is third-party**, nothing was downloaded, and none of them depicts a
real place or person. They are covered by the repository's MIT `LICENSE` and
carry no obligation for `npm run check:licences` to record.

**Two files came off the owner's phone** and are the owner's own work,
contributed under the same licence:

| File                  | Provenance                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `heic-with-gps.heic`  | An iPhone photograph of an iPad displaying a Max watchlist. 4032×3024, 1.76 MiB. **Coordinates redacted — see below.**                 |
| `ios-screenshot.jpeg` | An iOS screenshot of the Max _My Stuff / My List_ screen. Contains no name, no handle and no account identifier; the avatar is a logo. |

### 🔒 Why `heic-with-gps.heic`'s coordinates are redacted

`saquibrashid/nextup` is a **public** repository. As supplied, the file carried
the owner's real latitude, longitude and altitude. Committing that publishes it
to public git history permanently — deleting the file later does not retract
it.

[`redact-gps.mjs`](./redact-gps.mjs) therefore overwrote **four GPS tags in
place**, changing no offset and no length: `GPSLatitudeRef`, `GPSLatitude`,
`GPSLongitudeRef` and `GPSLongitude`, now pointing at a public landmark whose
degree, minute and second components are all non-zero (so the value can never
be misread as "GPS absent").

Everything the tests actually depend on is still exactly what the iPhone wrote:
the ISO-BMFF container, the EXIF item layout, IFD0, the Exif sub-IFD, the
device make and model, the XMP packet, the image raster, and the **other eleven
GPS tags**. This is redaction, not fabrication — a synthetic HEIC would prove
nothing, and this still proves everything.

The photograph itself was checked before commit: an indoor desk shot of a
tablet screen, with no window, address, document or face in frame.

| `heic-header.heic` _(same bytes)_      | `heic`    | **`application/octet-stream`**          | The iOS Safari case. Exposed as `heicAsOctetStream`.                                    |
| `heic-truncated.heic`                  | `heic`    | `image/heic`                            | Header intact, image data cut off. Decodes → `IMAGE_DECODE_FAILED`.                     |
| `heic-oversize.heic`                   | `heic`    | `image/heic`                            | Declares 8000×6000 (48.0 MP), over the 25 MP budget.                                    |
| `lying-blob.pdf`                       | _(none)_  | **`image/png`**                         | The lying-client case: a genuine PDF claiming to be an image.                           |
| `heic-with-gps.heic`                   | `heic`    | `application/octet-stream`              | **Real iPhone photo.** 15-tag GPS IFD + device model. Backs `T-SEC-033e/f/g`.           |
| `ios-screenshot.jpeg`                  | `jpeg`    | `image/jpeg`                            | **Real iOS screenshot.** EXIF but no GPS. Backs `T-SEC-032l/m`.                         |

`declaredContentType` is recorded in the manifest **so a test can hand a lie to
the pipeline and assert the pipeline ignored it**. It is never an input to a
decision: format is decided by sniffed magic bytes only.

Two `ispe` boxes appear in every HEIC stub, **the small one first**. A real
iPhone file carries several (thumbnail, depth/auxiliary images, one per burst
frame) and the first is frequently the thumbnail, so a header reader that took
the first match would report a fraction of a megapixel and wave a 48 MP master
straight past the pixel guard — while passing every single-`ispe` fixture on
the way. `T-IMG-013g` is what makes that falsifiable.

## What the synthetic `.heic` stubs are, and are not

They are **container-accurate headers**: a real ISO-BMFF `ftyp` box with a
HEIF-family brand list, and a real `meta` → `iprp` → `ipco` → `ispe` tree. That
is enough to exercise the sniff, the dimension read, the pixel guard and — for
`heic-truncated.heic` — a **real `heic-convert` decode failure**, offline, with
nothing injected.

They contain **no decodable HEVC image item**, because this repository cannot
produce one: `T-DEP-002` forbids a HEIC **encoder** anywhere in the dependency
tree (patent exposure and a GPL licence floor). Real HEIC decode, real
transcode and a real EXIF strip on real HEIC are asserted only against
`heic-with-gps.heic`, which is exactly why an owner-supplied file was needed.

## ⚠ Never assert EXIF presence by searching for tag bytes

The obvious way to check "does this carry GPS" is to look for the two bytes of
tag `0x8825`. **It does not work on real files.** In `heic-with-gps.heic` those
two bytes occur **33 times little-endian and 38 times big-endian** by pure
coincidence inside compressed image data; in `ios-screenshot.jpeg`, 6 and 2. An
assertion built that way passes or fails by chance, and keeps "passing" if the
stripper is deleted.

Use [`exifProbe.ts`](./exifProbe.ts), which parses the TIFF header, walks IFD0,
follows the GPS pointer and reports tag **presence** — exact in both
directions. It never returns or logs a coordinate value.

Related trap: **do not search a HEIF file for the string `Exif\0\0`**. It
occurs at least twice, and the first hit is the item _type_ recorded in an
`infe` box, not a payload — 126 KB away from the real data. Scan for the TIFF
magic instead.

## ⚠ On the HEIC path the metadata strip is not what keeps the blob clean

`transcodeHeicToPng` decodes to a raw raster and re-encodes, so metadata cannot
survive it. The stored blob is clean **whether or not `stripAllMetadata` runs**
— `T-SEC-033f` would keep passing if the strip were deleted outright.
`T-SEC-033g` proves that deliberately, by running the same real fixture with the
strip replaced by an identity function.

This matches `specs/testing.md` §29.2: the transcode's incidental metadata loss
is **not** what discharges REQ-078. The strip's own evidence comes from the PNG
and JPEG paths (`T-SEC-032i/j/k/m`), where bytes pass through un-re-encoded and
the strip is the only thing between EXIF and the blob store.

## Finding: iOS screenshots are not necessarily PNG

`.github/copilot-instructions.md` invariant 11 and ASM-058 both reason from
"iOS **screenshots** are normally PNG, iOS **camera photos** default to HEIC".
On the owner's device, screenshots save as **JPEG** — `ios-screenshot.jpeg` is
a genuine one.

The **conclusion is unaffected and reinforced**: accept PNG and JPEG and HEIC,
all three, and decide format by magic bytes rather than by filename or declared
type. Only the supporting rationale is wrong. Recorded here rather than fixed:
`specs/**` is outside this lane.
